summary: Russia is the largest country in the world by area, spanning Eastern Europe and northern Asia and covering 11 time zones; it is known for its literature, ballet and the vast expanse of Siberia.

ranking.name: Russian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In 988 Grand Prince Vladimir of Kievan Rus' was baptized and introduced Orthodoxy from Byzantium, laying the religious foundation of Russia. The Moscow Patriarchate was established in 1589, and Orthodoxy became the state religion of Tsarist Russia. After the October Revolution of 1917 the Bolsheviks promoted atheism, demolished large numbers of churches and executed clergy, and the Church was almost destroyed. After the celebration of the millennium of the baptism in 1988, religion gradually revived, and after the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 Orthodoxy recovered rapidly and cooperated closely with the state; many people regard Orthodoxy as part of Russian national identity, but the proportion who actually attend church regularly is not high.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From 1917 to 1991 the Soviet Union pursued state atheism, schools taught scientific atheism and religious activity was strictly restricted, so that several generations grew up in an environment without religious education. Although many people have identified with Orthodoxy again since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, a considerable proportion still have no religious belief, especially in large cities and among the highly educated.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced to the Volga Bulgaria khanate in 922, and in the 13th to 15th centuries the Golden Horde also converted to Islam. After Ivan IV conquered the Khanate of Kazan in 1552, Muslim peoples such as the Tatars were incorporated into Russia. In the 19th century Russia conquered the North Caucasus, and the Muslims of places such as Chechnya and Dagestan resisted for a long time. Today Muslims are concentrated in Tatarstan, Bashkortostan and the North Caucasus, and with migrants from Central Asia, Moscow also has a large number of Muslims.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: Other Christian denominations include Catholicism, Lutheranism, the Baptists and Pentecostals. Catholicism and Lutheranism were brought mainly by the Germans and Poles who immigrated from the 18th century at the invitation of Catherine II, and the Volga Germans were an important Protestant community. The Old Believers are an Orthodox group that split off in the 17th century in opposition to the religious reforms of Patriarch Nikon, and they still exist today.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism is mainly Tibetan Buddhism, introduced from Mongolia in the 17th and 18th centuries to Buryatia, Kalmykia and Tuva. In 1741 Empress Elizabeth recognized Buddhism as a legitimate religion in Russia. In the Soviet period monasteries were closed and lamas persecuted, and from the 1990s Buddhism gradually revived; the Republic of Kalmykia is the only region in Europe with a predominantly Buddhist population.

religion.background: In 988 Kievan Rus' accepted Orthodoxy, and Orthodoxy became the core of Russian culture. During Mongol rule in the 13th century, Islam spread in the Golden Horde. After the rise of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, Orthodoxy became closely bound up with state power, and the patriarchate was established in 1589. After the revolution of 1917 the Soviet Union pursued state atheism and religion was severely persecuted. After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 religion revived, and Orthodoxy, Islam, Buddhism and Judaism were recognized by law as Russia's traditional religions.

language.official: Russian is the official language of the whole country, and each republic additionally has its own local official language.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian belongs to the East Slavic branch and descends from the Old East Slavic of Kievan Rus'; after the rise of the Grand Duchy of Moscow it developed into the standard language on the basis of the Moscow dialect. In the 18th century Lomonosov codified the grammar, and in the 19th century Pushkin established the modern Russian literary language. In the Tsarist and Soviet periods Russian was promoted as the language common to the whole country, and all schools were required to teach it, so Russian is the mother tongue of the great majority and the common language among the various peoples.

ranking.name: Tatar
ranking.description: Tatar belongs to the Turkic family and is the language of the Volga Tatars, Russia's second largest ethnic group. After the Khanate of Kazan was conquered in 1552, the Tatars kept their own language and Islamic culture. After the Tatar Autonomous Republic was established in 1920, Tatar became the republic's official language. In 2017 the Russian government made the republics' languages optional in schools, which aroused the discontent of the Tatars.

ranking.name: Bashkir
ranking.description: Bashkir belongs to the Turkic family and is the language of the Bashkirs of the southern Urals, close to Tatar. The Bashkirs submitted to Russia in the 16th century and rose in revolt several times in the 18th century against Russian seizures of their land. After the Bashkir Autonomous Republic was established in 1919, Bashkir became the republic's official language, but the use of Russian in cities is becoming increasingly common.

language.history: Russian descends from Old East Slavic, and the Glagolitic alphabet created by Saints Cyril and Methodius in the 9th century and the later Cyrillic alphabet came with Orthodoxy. After the rise of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, the Moscow dialect became the basis of the standard language. In 1708 Peter the Great carried out a civil script reform, and in 1918 the Soviet government simplified spelling. In the Soviet period Russian became the common language of the whole country and the Union republics, and today there are still more than a hundred minority languages within Russia.

ranking.name: Pelmeni
ranking.description: Thin dough wrappers are filled with a mixture of pork, beef and lamb, pinched into small rounds, boiled, and eaten with sour cream, butter or vinegar.
ranking.history: Pelmeni originated in the Ural and Siberian regions, and the name comes from the language of the Komi or Udmurt peoples of the Urals, meaning 'ear of dough'. It is generally thought that the dumpling method was introduced via the Mongols or Central Asia. In the bitterly cold Siberian winters, people would make large batches of pelmeni and keep them frozen outdoors, and they could also be carried on long journeys; they are one of the most representative home dishes of Russia.

ranking.name: Blini (pancakes)
ranking.description: A batter of flour, milk and eggs is fried in a pan into thin pancakes, which can be eaten rolled around caviar, sour cream, jam or a meat filling.
ranking.history: Blini are among Russia's oldest foods and can be traced back to the pagan Slavic period before the arrival of Christianity; their round golden appearance is thought to symbolize the sun. During Maslenitsa, the 'Butter Week' before the Orthodox Great Lent, people make large quantities of blini to celebrate the passing of winter and the coming of spring, and at the end of the festival a straw effigy is burned. The traditions of this festival continue to this day.

ranking.name: Shchi (cabbage soup)
ranking.description: A soup based mainly on cabbage or sauerkraut, simmered with beef, carrots, onions and herbs, with a sour and savory taste, eaten with sour cream and rye bread.
ranking.history: Shchi is one of Russia's oldest soups, in existence since around the 9th century, and cabbage is easy to grow and store in Russia's cold climate. There is a Russian proverb, 'Shchi and kasha are our food', which shows its importance in the daily diet of the peasants. In the 19th century it passed from the countryside to the tables of the nobility, and it remains a common winter soup in Russian homes today.

ranking.name: Beef Stroganoff
ranking.description: Strips of beef are quickly sautéed and then simmered in a sauce of sour cream, onion, mushrooms and mustard, often served with mashed potatoes or noodles.
ranking.history: Beef Stroganoff is named after the Stroganov noble family of 19th-century Russia, and the earliest recipe appeared in a classic Russian cookbook published in 1871, combining French sauce techniques with Russian sour cream. After the revolution of 1917, many Russian exiles took the dish to China, Europe and the United States, making it an internationally famous dish.

ranking.name: Olivier salad
ranking.description: Boiled potatoes, carrots, pickled cucumbers, peas, boiled eggs and ham or chicken are cut into small cubes and mixed with mayonnaise, with a rich flavor.
ranking.history: Olivier salad was invented in the 1860s by the Belgian-born chef Lucien Olivier, who ran the Hermitage restaurant in Moscow; the original used expensive ingredients such as grouse, crayfish and caviar, and the recipe was never made public. In the Soviet period, because expensive ingredients were hard to obtain, cheaper ingredients such as potatoes and sausage were substituted, and it became an indispensable dish on the New Year's Eve table; abroad it is also called 'Russian salad'.
